01 Project Overview

This document describes the design, build, and operation of a Windows Server 2019 Active Directory homelab. The lab simulates a small multi-site enterprise environment with a single Domain Controller (Olwam.local), regional organizational units, domain users and groups, Group Policy management, file services with quotas and file screening, and a Windows 10 Enterprise client joined to the domain.

Several real-world incidents were encountered and resolved along the way — evaluation license expiration, a Group Policy misconfiguration that locked out the Domain Administrator, APIPA networking issues, and virtual network segmentation between the VMs. Each incident is documented below with root cause analysis and remediation steps.

Lab Inventory

Domain ControllerWindows Server 2019 Standard (Evaluation), hostname WIN-NUJ0MPC5RDE
ClientWindows 10 Enterprise (evaluation), VMware Workstation VM
Domain / ForestOlwam.local
HypervisorVMware Workstation (both VMs on a shared NAT network)
NetworkServer: 192.168.1.10 (static, DNS 127.0.0.1)  |  Client: static IP, DNS 192.168.1.10
Key RolesAD DS, DNS, File Server + File Server Resource Manager (FSRM)

02 Active Directory Structure

2.1 Organizational Units

Top-level OUs were created for three regions — Africa, Europe, and USA — each containing Users, Computers, and Servers sub-OUs. Department OUs (HR, IT, JSS) and a GP-TEST OU were also created for policy testing.

2.2 Groups and Users

Two groups were created in the USA OU to demonstrate both Active Directory group types, followed by four domain user accounts (East, North, South, and West Charmer).

GroupDL-ItAdmins — Distribution Group (Global) — email/distribution list, no security permissions
GroupIT — Security Group (Global) — used to assign permissions and user rights

03 License Lifecycle Management

Objective & Challenge

The Windows Server 2019 evaluation license was approaching expiration with 38 days remaining. Left unmanaged, the Windows License Monitoring Service (WLMS) would trigger hard shutdowns every 60 minutes, disrupting domain authentication, client connectivity, and lab operations.

Resolution Steps

  1. Audited the licensing state with the Software Licensing Management Tool: 
    slmgr /dlv
    This displayed the Windows Script Host diagnostics, confirming the evaluation channel and the remaining rearm count.
  2. Reset the evaluation clock: 
    slmgr /rearm
  3. Rebooted the Domain Controller to finalize the change, restoring a full 180-day evaluation period.
Key takeawayProactive license monitoring and command-line administration (slmgr) mirror real-world infrastructure lifecycle management: monitor compliance, maintain uptime, and act before the clock runs out.

04 Group Policy Objects

Six GPOs were created and configured as summarised below. Link-placement lessons learned from two of them are covered in Section 6.

Password PolicyScope: Domain — Min password age 90 days, min length 12, complexity enabled
Drive MappingScope: Users — Drive E: mapped to \\servername\folder
Desktop WallpaperScope: Users — Default wallpaper enforced for all users
Restrict Control PanelScope: Users — Prohibit access to Control Panel and PC settings
Disable USB StorageScope: Computers — All Removable Storage classes: deny all access
Account Lockout PolicyScope: Domain — Duration 10 min, threshold 10 attempts, reset counter 10 min

05 Windows 10 Client Deployment

A clean Windows 10 Enterprise VM was provisioned in VMware Workstation as a managed endpoint for domain onboarding and Group Policy deployment.

06 Incident Reports & Remediation

6.1 Incident 1 — Administrative Policy Lockout

SymptomThe Domain Administrator suddenly received "This operation has been cancelled due to restrictions in effect on this computer" when opening Control Panel, the Settings app, and Server Manager — and the desktop background turned solid black.
Root causeWhile configuring the domain-wide Password Policy GPO, the administrative template "Prohibit access to Control Panel and PC settings" was accidentally enabled inside that same GPO under User Configuration. Because the GPO was linked at the domain root (Olwam.local), the restriction inherited down to every object — including the built-in Administrator.
Resolution
  1. Bypassed the GUI restrictions by launching the Group Policy Management Console directly from the Run dialog: 
    gpmc.msc
  2. Edited the root-linked Password Policy GPO: User Configuration → Policies → Administrative Templates → Control Panel.
  3. Set "Prohibit access to Control Panel and PC settings" back to Not Configured.
  4. Forced a policy refresh, which completed successfully: 
    gpupdate /force
Key takeawayKeep GPOs granular. Universal policies (like password complexity) should never contain restrictive user-environment settings. Restrictive GPOs must be linked only to lower-level sub-OUs (e.g., HR, IT) to prevent administrative lockout.

6.2 Incident 2 — Network Adapter "Permission Block" & APIPA

Phase 1 — Permission blockOpening "Change adapter options" in the Settings app on the server threw the same restriction error. Two factors collided: (1) the Restrict Control Panel and Disable USB Storage GPOs were linked at the domain root, trapping the Domain Administrator; and (2) UAC Admin Approval Mode is disabled by default for the built-in Administrator on a DC, breaking modern Settings-app links while policies are active.
FixDeleted the root-level links for the two restrictive GPOs, enabled "UAC: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator" (secpol.msc → Local Policies → Security Options), ran gpupdate /force, and rebooted.
Phase 2 — APIPA (169.254.x.x)ipconfig showed an autoconfiguration address (169.254.40.250) and pings from the Windows 10 client returned "Destination host unreachable." Root cause: the server VM was in VMware Bridged mode while the client was on NAT, placing them on separate virtual networks — and the server was set to DHCP with no reachable DHCP server.
Fix
  • Assigned a static IP via ncpa.cpl: 192.168.1.10 / 255.255.255.0, Preferred DNS 127.0.0.1, no default gateway (isolated lab)
  • Switched both VMs to the same NAT network in VMware Workstation
  • Disabled Windows Defender Firewall on all three profiles (firewall.cpl) for lab connectivity
  • Result: ping 192.168.1.10 from the client returned 4 successful responses, 0% packet loss
Phase 3 — Domain join
  1. Set a static IP on the Windows 10 client with Preferred DNS = 192.168.1.10 — the critical step that lets the client discover Olwam.local
  2. Ran sysdm.cpl on the client, selected Domain, and entered Olwam.local
  3. Authenticated with the server's Administrator credentials; the machine object was created in AD and the client rebooted
Phase 4 — ValidationSigned in as a domain user (eastcharmer) and verified the applied policies: 
gpresult /r

07 File Services, Share Permissions & Drive Mapping

7.1 Creating the Shared Folder

A folder named SHARED was created on the server's C: drive. Share and NTFS permissions were configured so that Domain Users can read the folder across the network: Share Permissions grant Everyone Read access, and Domain Users were added explicitly.

7.2 Manual Drive Mapping (Non-Persistent)

From the Windows 10 client, the share was mapped manually via Map Network Drive using the server hostname (retrieved with the hostname command), assigned drive letter S. This works but is not persistent for daily use — hence the GPO-based mapping that follows.

7.3 Persistent Drive Mapping via Group Policy

  1. Created a new GPO named "Mapped Drivers" in the Group Policy Objects container
  2. Configured User Configuration → Preferences → Windows Settings → Drive Maps: Action = Update, Location = \\WIN-NUJ0MPC5RDE\SHARED, Label = SHARED, drive letter S
  3. Linked the GPO to the USA → USERS OU
  4. On the client, forced the policy: 
    gpupdate /force

08 File Server Resource Manager (FSRM)

The File Server Resource Manager feature was installed to enforce storage limits and block unauthorized file types.

8.1 Quotas

A custom hard quota was created on C:\SHARED (limit 100 MB), with a notification threshold at 80% and an email alert configured to notify administrators as usage approaches the limit.

8.2 File Screening

A file screen was applied to C:\SHARED using Active screening ("Do not allow users to save unauthorized files") with the Block Audio and Video Files template — blocking audio/video, compressed, executable, and image files to preserve disk space.

09 Security Hardening (Default Domain Policy)

9.1 Password Policy

Enforce password history4 passwords remembered
Maximum password age60 days
Minimum password age1 day
Minimum password length7 characters
Password must meet complexity requirementsEnabled
Store passwords using reversible encryptionDisabled

9.2 Account Lockout Policy

Account lockout duration30 minutes
Account lockout threshold3 invalid logon attempts
Allow Administrator account lockoutEnabled
Reset account lockout counter after30 minutes

9.3 User Rights Assignment

A GPO named "User Rights" was created to demonstrate rights-based access control:

  • "Deny log on locally" — applied to the IT group (OLWAM\IT): IT staff cannot log on interactively at machines where the GPO applies
  • "Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services" — applied to OLWAM\IT: IT staff administer systems via RDP only

10 Summary & Lessons Learned

  • Designed a multi-region AD structure (Africa, Europe, USA) with Users/Computers/Servers sub-OUs, both group types, and test users
  • Managed the Windows Server evaluation license lifecycle with slmgr /dlv and slmgr /rearm (180-day reset)
  • Deployed six functional GPOs covering passwords, lockout, drive mapping, wallpaper, USB blocking, and Control Panel restrictions
  • Diagnosed and resolved a self-inflicted Domain Administrator lockout — the classic lesson in GPO granularity and link placement
  • Built a functioning two-VM network (static IPs, DNS pointed at the DC, unified NAT mode, firewall rules) and joined Windows 10 to Olwam.local
  • Delivered file services end-to-end: NTFS/share permissions, persistent GPO drive mapping, FSRM quotas with alerts, and file screening
  • Applied security baselines (password policy, lockout thresholds, user rights) mirroring real enterprise standards
Next stepsExtend the lab with a second Domain Controller for replication, DHCP on the server, a WSUS/backup strategy, and fine-grained password policies per OU.
